html:
The Miraña (Miranha in Portuguese) are an Indigenous people of the forest between the Caquetá, or Japurá, river and the Putumayo, on the border of Colombia and Brazil. They speak a dialect of the Bora language.

In the early 1800s European travellers described them as a powerful people who took captives from their neighbours and sold them to Portuguese traders. The naturalist Carl von Martius took two children from the region, a Miraña girl among them, back to Munich in 1820, where both soon died. A century later the Miraña and their Bora relatives suffered greatly in the Putumayo atrocities of the rubber boom.
